prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching accuracy and stability that enable new tests of fundamental physics and a redefinition of the second

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a concrete invention with a clear origin: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the light-shift problem that blocked neutral-atom optical clocks, and Ye's group then drove accuracy and stability to roughly 1e-18, now beyond the caesium definition of the second. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories with strontium, ytterbium and other species, and it opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to a new SI second. That fits the 'discovery or invention' criterion I take seriously, and a two-person prize has an unusually clean credit boundary. It is also the one candidate that two members placed first and that I can support without relying on my own subfield. My opening first choice, aberration-corrected TEM, remains scientifically strong, but I should not press it as the lead given my proximity to the field, so I move B010 to the front.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is that the clock story is not cleanly separable from optical frequency combs (recognised in 2005) and from ion clocks, so some colleagues may see it as partly honoured already. Other lattice-clock pioneers (for example Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and theory contributors such as Derevianko) are outside a two-name credit, and the relative weight of Katori's proposal versus Ye's accuracy programme is a judgement call. The pending redefinition of the second does not weaken the science, but the committee may prefer to wait for it. The thin opening support for my own B039 and the broad support for B047 and B051 also mean B010 is not an obvious consensus pick.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first, with Katori proposing and first realising the magic-wavelength scheme and Ye carrying it to the highest accuracy, while noting that ion-clock and frequency-comb work may belong to the same story.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the maturity argument. I would qualify the overlap concern: the comb prize rewarded the measurement tool, whereas the lattice clock is a distinct scheme that uses it, and ion clocks are a different physical route with different systematics. A citation that names the lattice clock specifically avoids double-counting. I do not think the ion-clock community has a claim that displaces Katori and Ye here, though it is a fair thing to record as an uncertainty.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B010 first and stresses that two laureates fit cleanly, that the technology is about two decades old and independently confirmed, and that the weighting of Katori's proposal against Ye's accuracy milestones is a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree that two names are sufficient and that independent confirmation is strong. On the judgement call, I would not rank proposal over accuracy: the proposal is what made a competitive neutral-atom clock possible, and the accuracy record is what turned it into a metrological and fundamental-physics instrument. Both are prize-level. I am less persuaded that her second choice, topological insulators, is better placed, because the allocation problem around Mele, Bernevig and Hasan is much harder than anything in B010.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the quantum spin Hall and topological insulator work first for its conceptual novelty, a topological invariant replacing broken symmetry, but notes that the 2016 prize already covered topological phases and that the HgTe and 3D contributions complicate credit.
responses.response: I take the conceptual argument seriously; it is the deepest idea on the list. My disagreement is about readiness of the configuration rather than merit. With the 2016 prize close by and Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan all plausible but Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left out, any three or four names will be contested. I would only move to B047 if the committee can settle the credit, and I would keep it as an alternative, not a lead.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on its influence for superconducting processors, but questions whether a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 is wise and flags that the omitted Girvin and Huang complicate allocation.
responses.response: I share his doubt about recency: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a quick return to the area hard to justify, and the omission of Girvin and Huang is a real attribution problem, so I would keep B041 out of my configuration. I also respect his own statement that his subfield should lower his weight on it, and I apply the same discipline to myself on electron microscopy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and from ion-clock work.
How to treat other lattice-clock pioneers outside the two-name credit; I am relying on recollection of the history of the magic-wavelength proposal.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising the work.
Whether aberration-corrected STEM, a parallel development not in the supplied B039 credit, would complicate that configuration if it were advanced.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B039 (aberration-corrected TEM) as an alternative and have a professional proximity to transmission electron microscopy through my own research and the international microscopy federation, so I would recuse myself from any decision on that candidate and have not led with it. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which is relevant for a concrete conflict check on B041; I have no specific personal connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names apparent from my profile.
